query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a hybrid computational approach that combines machine learning with reduced-order modeling will significantly reduce the computational cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties while maintaining accuracy.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid and fluid states of multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.intervention: Utilize machine learning algorithms to predict free energies and relevant entropy terms based on a limited set of high-fidelity ab initio calculations.
generation.conditions: The approach will be tested across various multicomponent high-entropy systems at temperatures ranging from room temperature to their respective melting points.
generation.structural_mediator: Machine learning models trained on a database of computed free energies and entropy terms.
generation.mechanism: The machine learning models will learn the relationships between structural features and thermodynamic properties, allowing for rapid predictions without the full computational cost of molecular dynamics.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in computational time (potentially by an order of magnitude) while achieving fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
generation.baseline: Current methodologies using explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD for high-entropy systems.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis will be tested for multicomponent high-entropy alloys at temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K.
generation.uncertainty: The accuracy of the machine learning predictions may vary depending on the quality and quantity of training data available.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the predicted free energies and derived thermodynamic properties from the hybrid approach against those obtained from explicit ab initio molecular dynamics for the same systems.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid approach deviates from the ab initio results by more than 5% for any key thermodynamic property, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
